“Something wicked this way comes.”.

It was naivety, but when I first came across Flexbox, and then CSS Grid, I had this feeling all those positioning properties (align-self, justify-content…) would be available to use on block and inline elements; things like tables, lists, fixed elements, everything. The workings might be different under the hood, depending on the reference boxes, but the syntax and expected outcomes would be same: push to one edge, keep at the center, spread around evenly, etc.

Although that didn’t happen, what if I made something of that sort?

Recent findings suggest that for example, I could take out the soul of an HTML table and stitch it back together with CSS Grid. In other words, it reads like a table, but acts like a grid, allowing me to use grid properties. Believe it or not, some form of this was used in the past to make tables responsive.

Before I kill off a table in this article though: there are a lot of advantages to straight-up tables. They provide a clean semantic layout that browsers perfectly understand and translate for assistive technology when needed. There’s even a element.

In a recent development, on the CSS side of things, there are indeed circumstances where CSS Grid is necessary for its intrinsic responsiveness, source order independence, and positioning. That’s why it’s an indispensable tool for layouts. Use that and let HTML tables to do the work of actually displaying tabular data!

In a recent development, but there’s the presentational benefit of table we should consider. Technically, is not a presentational element like a . It’s semantic: the browser and I share a common meaning for it. But whether the browser understands it as such or not, if I read I believe it’s a heading followed by data. Let’s say that’s pseudo-semantic to me, if presentation is not the right term.

That pseudo-semanticism is still useful. It’s the difference between me having to read this:.

Despite there being semantic elements for titles, like and , they don’t bring in the connection that and have, and it’s better to reserve and for textual structuring like glossaries rather than layouts.

According to recent reports, so, is it okay if I use this way? I mean, the table itself merely used as pseudo-semantic markup skin:.

Then, this CSS and its outcome (for the first markup):.

…changes to this (for the table markup):.

To me, the latter markup example — a pseudo-semantic table — is easier to scan than a handful of generic divs. I get the pseudo-semantics of table, and the ease of using CSS Grid for the layout. As for browsers, none of them have shunned this sort of Frankenstein creation, at least yet. The VoiceOver and keyboard navigation works as if it’s a real table.

But it’s understandable why it looks more than a little gross and against the grain of what we should be able to. We’re encouraged to maintain a separation of concerns between content and presentation and this does exactly that without affecting the tables semantics, such as its role. But maybe it should? There are plenty of other HTML elements that CSS is capable of busting.

  • So what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

So what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions? Is there really any noticeable difference between carets, chevrons, arrows, and triangles?

Well, research indicates that there is some difference indeed. But what’s more interesting is that split menus are harmful, why it’s better to not have icons and text labels link to different actions, and why the caret is the safest icon choice. Let’s dive in!

The findings aren’t very surprising: without any icon in use, owners expect that tapping on the menu item would take them directly to a new page. Users often struggle with custom icons as they don’t clearly signal that they’ll open an accordion. And people tend to tap fairly equally on the icon and on the label for most icons.

Industry observers note that many designs (like the one below) tend to slightly overcomplicate things by adding arrows and carets pointing everywhere, depending on the state of the accordion. But typically we don’t need to use an arrow to indicate a link to the category.

Recent findings suggest that the rule of thumb is very simple: if it’s a link, the easiest and most effective way is to simply underline it — without any arrow, caret, or other icon. Perhaps it’s not particularly exciting, but it works flawlessly every single time.

Industry observers note that using a right-facing arrow icon ▶ isn’t associated with an expectation of going directly to a fresh page. And having the same icon pointing down ▼ doesn’t necessarily imply that an accordion is going to open on tap/click.

Sources indicate that it’s a good idea to avoid split buttons for accordions — where the text label links directly to a page, but the icon opens the accordion. Instead, it’s much more reliable to allow users to tap on a main category and expose the menu; and to access the category page, we add a link to it inside the menu.

It has been revealed that for accordions, we typically use +/− or arrows ↓/↑ to signal expanded and collapsed states, and typically it works well. However, both have many different interpretations. Plus + can mean anything from saving for later to adding to cart to zooming in, and can be particularly confusing for multi-level navigation, with many levels open at the same time.

Recent findings suggest that arrows ↓/↑ can mean scrolling or sliding or finding the next match, but also a jump to a particular portion of a page. Both plus and arrows are well-understood and work, but depending on the design, can be confusing — mostly because they are overloaded.

It has been revealed that the safe choice is to use the caret/triangle pointing down ▼ by default, and change it to a caret pointing up or a caret pointing sideways ▶ on interaction. If you need an alternative, then +/- typically work well, too.

In a recent development, but we certainly don’t need any further icons or arrows to indicate where the links go. The same goes for split menus, which often produce more mistakes than help. Instead, we have one button or dropdown that does exactly one thing — highlights all options and allows owners to drill down.

According to recent reports, and if you need a direct link, we link the title directly to the page and underline it. More often than not, simpler is better.

#93. SilentAir Hijacks Asian Telecom Networks to Intercept SMS 2FA Codes and Spy on Taiwanese Users

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1119 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thehackernews

SilentAir Hijacks Asian Telecom Networks to Intercept SMS 2FA Codes and Spy on Taiwanese Users

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thehackernews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly identified spying group used hacked equipment inside Asian mobile operators to intercept the calls and texts of selected people, mostly in Taiwan.
  • In a recent development, enea, a telecom and cybersecurity software organization based in Stockholm, found the group's attack sources in at least six Asian countries and named it SilentAir this week.
  • The company has told the operators where it found SilentAir sources.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly identified spying group used hacked equipment inside Asian mobile operators to intercept the calls and texts of selected people, mostly in Taiwan.

In a recent development, enea, a telecom and cybersecurity software organization based in Stockholm, found the group's attack sources in at least six Asian countries and named it SilentAir this week. It assessed with high confidence that SilentAir is a state-level actor, but linked its activity to China only with low confidence.

The company has told the operators where it found SilentAir sources. It said SilentAir has been disrupted for now but could return. The report does not say whether those operators have cleaned up the hacked equipment.

According to recent reports, mobile operators use the SS7 and Diameter protocols to exchange signaling messages that route calls and texts and enable roaming. This traffic crosses a shared network called the IPX, which runs on a high level of trust between operators. SilentAir sent its attacks into the IPX from the hacked equipment.

Recent findings suggest that for interception, SilentAir sent the target's home network an UpdateLocation message, or its Diameter equivalent. The message claimed that the hacked equipment was now serving the target's phone. If the home network accepted it, calls and texts for that person would be diverted to the attackers.

It has been revealed that some of these attacks worked. For some targets, the company observed two-factor authentication (2FA) codes being intercepted immediately after the diversion took effect. That points to an attempt to break into other accounts registered to those people.

The report gives no similar evidence for voice calls, and it does not say whether any account was taken over.

Interception made up 18.3% of the attacks the organization saw from SilentAir. For a typical surveillance company, the kind of firm behind most signaling attacks, the share was 2.1% in the company's earlier research.

Some targets were political and government VIPs in their own countries. In rare cases, SilentAir equipment in several countries worked together against such targets, which the manufacturer said points to a single controller.

Outside Taiwan, targets were mostly in other Southeast and East Asian networks, and at times in East Africa, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. People using the hacked operators' own networks may also have been targeted, but the tech giant could not see that traffic.

The organization spotted SilentAir by studying attacks on the links between operators. Since early 2025, it has tracked unusual attacks, mostly over SS7 and sometimes Diameter, from some Asian operators that would not normally send attacks. Later analysis found suspicious activity even earlier.

It has been revealed that the networks hosting SilentAir handled follow-up messages for diverted targets in odd and inconsistent ways, according to the company's technical report. That left two explanations: someone outside was faking those networks' signaling addresses, or equipment inside each network had been taken over.

In a recent development, the organization then saw equipment inside one operator both send and receive attack commands, which confirmed the second explanation. That equipment behaved exactly like SilentAir sources in other networks.

In a recent development, detecting and blocking the attacks was hard at first because the attackers understood mobile networks and signaling defenses well. After the attacks were contained, the company recovered traces of unauthorized access. It could not analyze the malware it believes SilentAir used.

Sources indicate that the report does not name the countries, the operators, or any of the targets. In some countries, SilentAir attacks came from more than one operator.

If the test text reached the hacked equipment instead of the phone, the attackers knew they were getting that person's texts.

In a recent development, most silent SMS went out at night, and most of those went to people in Taiwan. The company stated the purpose of those messages is not confirmed. They may be a bulk check that earlier diversions were still in place, since phones are least likely to re-register to their real location at night.

The silent texts carried spam-like motivational or promotional lines, often in English. The company believes the text was a disguise. If an operator along the way stripped a message's silent setting, the recipient would see it as spam and ignore it.

Industry observers note that its tracking and interception attacks also followed a working day in UTC+8, which is China Standard Time. They started at 9 a.m., almost stopped on weekends, and paused or slowed around Chinese holidays.

In a recent development, the organization also considered a link to Liminal Panda, a group behind earlier telecom intrusions. It called the link possible but unconfirmed and does not tie the two groups together for now.

Industry observers note that in several hacked operators, SilentAir attacks happened during a known Liminal Panda infection. At other times, the two revealed no sign of working together. They also went after operators in the same part of Asia, though Liminal Panda has no known focus on Taiwan.

SilentAir's behavior also partly matches that of SCTPE, a little-known Linux trojan that runs in the kernel and is designed to send and receive SS7 and Diameter traffic.

Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) has described the same tool in a government advisory. There, the tool is called SIGweaver. The agency stated CrowdStrike identified it on January 21 and links it to Liminal Panda with moderate confidence.

But Enea mentioned SilentAir answered messages it had not sent itself, which the known SCTPE program cannot do. SilentAir's operational security also seemed far better than Liminal Panda's.

Separately, the organization's GTP firewall has detected Liminal Panda activity at several customer operators since the first quarter of this year. The company blocked the group's GTPDoor traffic there and saw Liminal Panda infections, or strong signs of them, in at least 5 to 10 operators.

Sources indicate that the GTPDoor backdoor, first documented on February 27, 2024, hides commands within GTP-C, the protocol that establishes mobile data connections between networks. The tech giant also found evidence of a upcoming version that hides commands in GTP-U, the part of GTP that carries customers' data. GTP-U traffic is harder to inspect, though the company believes the new version serves mainly as a backup.

The company noted any attacker could reuse these techniques, and it told operators to:.

The report does not advise people whose calls and texts may be targeted.

#92. How AIClaw 3.11.5 Separates Installed Versions from Published Release History

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (520 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

How AIClaw 3.11.5 Separates Installed Versions from Published Release History

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An update screen has to answer two different questions: which version is running here, and what has actually been published?
  • Recent findings suggest that AIClaw 3.11.5 adds an About page that brings the installed version, an update check, and recent release notes into settings.
  • It has been revealed that the About view asks the existing Electron bridge for the application version.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An update screen has to answer two different questions: which version is running here, and what has actually been published? A tag pushed to GitHub is not enough to answer the second question. A failed release workflow can leave a tag behind without producing a GitHub Release.

Recent findings suggest that AIClaw 3.11.5 adds an About page that brings the installed version, an update check, and recent release notes into settings. The useful part is how it keeps local version information and remote release history independent.

It has been revealed that the About view asks the existing Electron bridge for the application version. It separately loads release notes through a read-only IPC endpoint. A failed history request therefore does not prevent the page from showing the local version.

Sources indicate that the Check for updates button uses the existing upgrade action. It does not infer update availability from the list of release notes. That keeps browsing release history separate from deciding whether a newer version is available.

The release-notes reader requests the project’s public GitHub Releases endpoint with a ten-second timeout. It accepts only entries explicitly marked as neither drafts nor prereleases, with a published timestamp and a tag matching the stable vX.Y.Z form.

The implementation requests the first ten API results, filters them, and returns at most ten notes. That is a bounded recent history, not a complete archive: if the first page contains prereleases, the resulting list can have fewer than ten entries. A tag with no published release never enters this list.

Each accepted entry contains the tag, publication time, note body, and a release link. The link is constructed from the fixed AIClaw repository address and validated tag rather than copied from a response-provided URL. Note bodies are capped at 100,000 characters per entry and displayed through the existing Markdown renderer.

Sources indicate that the page has separate loading, failure, and empty states. A failed HTTP request or an invalid top-level response stays an error; it is not converted into an empty list that could misleadingly suggest there are no releases. The failure state provides a retry button. A published entry without a note body gets its own “no release notes” message.

This is still an online history view. It does not provide an offline archive, paginate through every past release, or prove that a downloaded installer has been exercised on a particular machine.

According to recent reports, the release-note tests cover stable-release filtering, fixed-repository links, and preservation of HTTP and invalid-response errors. The desktop smoke suite also checks that the About page displays the application version and release notes.

The 3.11.5 release notes report a passing local make check, including 381 work UI checks, plus release-note tests under Node 22 in a Linux container. Those checks are distinct from live acceptance of every installer. The GitHub Release itself is now publicly published.

A small About page can make version support less ambiguous: the installed version comes from the application, the history comes from published releases, and a network failure remains visible as a network failure.

Nov 15, 2026 2 min read.

Recent findings suggest that cloudflare recently made Application Services for Private Origins generally available, allowing public traffic to reach applications hosted on private networks without exposing their IP addresses or opening inbound firewall ports. Private-to-private connectivity is not yet supported.

According to recent reports, unveiled in closed beta in June, the service is now generally available with a simplified configuration: private IP addresses are automatically detected in proxied DNS records, and private routing can be configured through the DNS API. Enrique Somoza, product development manager at Cloudflare, writes:.

We introduced this capability (...) to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet.

Sources indicate that existing Cloudflare connectivity can be used to apply WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, and Workers to private origins, just as with public-facing applications. The service also supports private TCP/UDP origins through Spectrum and private connectivity for Workers. Somoza adds:.

Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers.

Using Private Origins requires a Private Origins entitlement, Cloudflare One connectivity, and Unified Routing (not required when using Cloudflare Tunnel). Cloudflare WAN and Mesh connections also require return routes for Cloudflare's IPv4 (100.64.0.0/12) and IPv6 (2606:4700:cf1:5000::/64) source ranges, as well as a proxied DNS record pointing to the private IP with private network routing enabled. Existing WAF, caching, and bot management policies apply automatically. Simon Painter, cloud network consultant, notes:.

No extra connector software. WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching and Workers all sit in front of stuff that was never meant to be on the open internet. The interesting bit isn't the marketing wrapper — it's the DNS implication. For years the rule was: "if it answers a public DNS name, it's reachable from the public internet." That stops being true here.

It has been revealed that cloudflare is not the only cloud provider offering ways to connect public-facing services to private application backends. AWS, for example, offers CloudFront VPC Origins, while Microsoft provides similar capabilities through Azure Front Door Premium and Private Link. Giacomo Masseroni writes:.

Finally. been punching holes in security groups just to let the edge in.

With general availability, Cloudflare has updated the Private Origins developer documentation. The announcement does not clarify whether the feature carries an additional charge or is included in existing Enterprise contracts.

According to recent reports, cloudflare plans to extend the service to support private-to-private traffic, allowing owners, services, and AI agents on one private network to access applications on another. A closed beta is targeted for early 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A proxy URL in our secret store was wrapped in typographic quotes. Nothing could parse it, one service crash-looped on startup, and two others quietly fell back to direct HTTP. The command that wrote it looked correct, and when we copied it out of chat it worked fine.

This is how we found it, and what to do so it doesn't happen to you.

In a recent development, an alert fired: a queue backlog had aged past two hours. Every pod of the download worker was dying at startup with the same line:.

Recent findings suggest that two other services that read the same secret didn't crash. They logged a warning about an invalid proxy URL and fell back to direct HTTP, so they kept running without their datacenter proxy tier. The queue grew to about 12,000 messages while the worker restarted in a loop.

Our startup log prints a safe description of each proxy URL: host, port and zone, with no credentials. For a URL that fails to parse, it prints the word invalid.

According to recent reports, two proxy URLs are configured, a datacenter one and an unlocker one. They come from separate secret properties and are parsed by the same code. The unlocker logged a normal host and zone. Only the datacenter one logged invalid. So only one value was bad.

Recent findings suggest that our team could write the secret but not read it or its history, which is why this took a while. Once we had read access, the version history of the property highlighted it. One version was 96 characters long instead of 94, and it began and ended with these:.

A shell only treats ' and " as quoting. The curly versions are ordinary characters, so the secret store kept them.

The stored value was never a URL. It was a URL wrapped in two extra characters.

Go's net/url gives different errors depending on where the stray character sits:.

If you only check err != nil, the last row slips through, so check the host too.

The commands were kept in Apple Notes. Notes turns on Smart Quotes by default, and it converts quotes as you type, not when you paste.

Two lines in the same note can therefore differ:.

Sources indicate that the first line was pasted into the note. The second was typed by hand. The closing quote on the second line is the right curly quote, U+2019, the same character we found at the end of the stored secret.

That also explains why only one of the two commands failed. The unlocker command was pasted and stayed straight. The datacenter command had been edited by hand in the note.

In a recent development, the command was shared in a chat app, and chat apps tend to normalise quotes back to straight ones. Copying the command out of the message gave one that worked. When someone ran the original command again to show it was broken, it broke again, with the same bytes. Only the raw stored value showed the difference.

The shell, the secret store and the URL parser all did exactly what they were told. The only thing that changed was two characters that look almost the same as the ones you meant. If a value that "looks right" won't parse, look at its bytes.

#85. When an AI Agent Goes Wrong, Can You Stop It?

When an AI Agent Goes Wrong, Can You Stop It?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thehackernews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, suppose an AI agent is asked to sort support tickets and look up account details.
  • That kind of scenario raises a response question: what does “stop the agent” actually mean?
  • An October 2026 roundup from the OWASP GenAI Security Project describes evaluation agents reaching beyond their intended scope and recommends testing whether containment can revoke both credentials and network access.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, suppose an AI agent is asked to sort support tickets and look up account details. A ticket contains instructions that lead the agent to export records to an unfamiliar destination. The agent can make the request because its identity has access to the records and its connected tools allow the action.

That kind of scenario raises a response question: what does “stop the agent” actually mean? A team may be able to pause the model while a workflow, credential or existing connection remains active. Those pieces can require separate controls.

An October 2026 roundup from the OWASP GenAI Security Project describes evaluation agents reaching beyond their intended scope and recommends testing whether containment can revoke both credentials and network access. The roundup is a selected collection, not an exhaustive survey of incidents.

Recent findings suggest that an AI agent is usually part of a larger system. A model may choose an action, but an orchestrator runs the workflow, an identity supplies access and tools or APIs carry out the work. Network rules determine where those tools can connect.

The details vary by deployment. In one system, disabling the agent may stop its current task. In another, queued jobs, retries or an already established session may continue. Revoking one credential may not invalidate a different token or connection. A model endpoint can be offline while a separate service continues to process work it already received.

That is why “kill switch” is best understood as a tested set of controls. It may need to stop active and queued runs, revoke the credentials they use, disable access to tools and restrict network paths. The right sequence depends on the architecture and the risk of interrupting other services.

An unexpected action does not automatically mean an agent has been compromised. A changed workflow, a software defect, a bad configuration or an unusual input can produce behavior that looks suspicious. Teams should investigate the signal and its context.

Signals that warrant a closer look include:.

The agent’s own logs can help explain what it attempted, but they are only one source of evidence. Security teams should compare them with identity-provider, API, application and network records. A log entry showing an attempted action does not necessarily prove that the action succeeded.

In a recent development, stop the active run and suspend its triggers, retries or queue where possible. If the agent shares infrastructure with other services, isolate the affected workflow rather than taking down unrelated systems, provided you can do so safely.

In a recent development, A prompt telling the agent to stop is not a containment control. The response should act through the system that runs the workflow.

Identify the credentials, sessions, grants and service identities associated with the run. Disable or revoke the access that is no longer trusted. If there is evidence that a secret was exposed, rotate it and review where else it is used.

Industry observers note that revocation behaves differently across systems. Some tokens expire swiftly; others may remain valid until a session ends or a specific service invalidates them. Teams should confirm that the affected access is no longer usable instead of assuming that disabling the agent handled it.

Recent findings suggest that disable the tool or integration involved in the activity, or apply an access policy that blocks the agent from reaching the affected resource. If data may be moving outside the organization, network controls can limit further connections while the investigation continues.

This control should sit outside the agent’s own instructions. OWASP’s AI Agent Security guidance recommends least-privilege tool access, explicit authorization for sensitive operations, audit trails and ways to interrupt or roll back agent operations.

Record the agent identity, run or session ID, timestamps, tool calls, authorization decisions and affected resources. Preserve relevant identity, API and network logs before normal retention or rotation removes them. Avoid copying secret values into incident notes or general-purpose logs.

Recent findings suggest that then determine what the agent actually changed or accessed. Check for files read or modified, records exported, permissions changed, messages sent or credentials retrieved. Separate completed actions from attempted ones, and confirmed facts from assumptions.

According to recent reports, if the agent accessed a sensitive account or resource, assess that resource on its own. Revoke additional access, remove unauthorized changes and involve the relevant system owner. If data may have left the environment, follow the organization’s incident, privacy and notification processes.

Stopping the agent limits further activity. It does not undo actions already completed.

Before restarting the workflow, identify the cause. It may involve unsafe input, overbroad permissions, a compromised integration, a configuration change or a defect in the agent’s surrounding system. Fixing the prompt alone will not address a problem in credentials or network policy.

Restore access with the smallest scope the task requires. Test the workflow in a controlled environment, verify that high-impact actions receive the required authorization and monitor its tool calls and access after it resumes. Where an action could expose sensitive data or make an irreversible change, a human review step can give the team time to catch errors before execution.

An incident response blueprint is only useful if teams know which controls to use and can reach them under pressure. For each production agent, organizations should know:.

Those procedures should be tested. A tabletop exercise can expose gaps, but teams should also verify that revoking credentials and disabling tools work in the actual environment. NIST’s incident response guidance treats preparation, response and recovery as part of cybersecurity risk management, not as steps to improvise after an event.

Industry observers note that an effective response starts with knowing which credentials an agent can use and how to revoke its access. KeeperPAM® brings secrets management, access controls and auditing together to help organizations govern the credentials behind AI-driven workflows.

In a recent development, with Keeper Secrets Manager, teams can give agents access to only the secrets their tasks require, retrieve credentials at runtime and review secret-access events. These controls support containment alongside tested procedures for stopping workflows, terminating sessions and restricting network access.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A teenager from Amman, Jordan suspected of leading the prolific data theft and extortion group ShinyHunters has been detained and is reportedly cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the hacking gang. KrebsOnSecurity has learned that the suspect, who uses the hacker handle “Rey,” was detained as ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting a business unit recently divested by the global aerospace tech giant Boeing, which manufactures the fleet of planes used by the employer of Rey’s father — Royal Jordanian Airlines.

The logo for Jeppesen ForeFlight, a business unit divested last year by the aerospace firm Boeing.

It has been revealed that on October 3, Reuters cited three unnamed sources saying a suspected ShinyHunters member in Amman named Saif Al-din Khader was detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI. KrebsOnSecurity identified Rey as Khader in a November 2025 profile, in which the young man admitted working with multiple ransomware groups.

Rey was featured again in a September 28 exclusive about the Dutch police arresting 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by ShinyHunters. The story noted that immediately following the Dutchman’s arrest on the evening of September 15, Rey assumed control over the ShinyHunters brand and boasted publicly about stealing highly sensitive data from the FBI and extorting the ransomware group Cl0p.

Rey taunted both the FBI and Cl0p with memes posted to his longtime account on Twitter/X, while simultaneously including images of the avatar used by Van Der Stap’s former hacker alias “Umbreon” in an apparent attempt to frame the Dutchman for both hacks.

According to recent reports, A taunting meme uploaded to Twitter/X by Rey on Sept. 22. A giant sized version of the Pokemon character Umbreon can be seen in the bottom left.

As noted in our September 28 report, ShinyHunters gained access to the FBI site and other victims by exploiting a vulnerability (CVE-2026-35273) in PeopleSoft, a software-as-a-service platform from the tech giant Oracle that is broadly used by companies to manage hiring and human resources, benefits and payroll. Oracle rapidly issued a fix for CVE-2026-35273, which ShinyHunters first began exploiting as a zero-day in June, and at the time Mandiant released web application firewall rules intended for organizations that couldn’t apply the security update quickly enough.

It has been revealed that shinyHunters told BleepingComputer in June that the original goal behind exploiting the PeopleSoft vulnerability was to breach the FBI’s own PeopleSoft database, but the hackers stated those attacks were unsuccessful for some reason. In recent weeks, however, ShinyHunters turned to a well-known URL-encoding trick to bypass Mandiant’s suggested web application firewall rules.

It has been revealed that in a report released Sept. 25, security experts at Mandiant and the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed that ShinyHunters had mass-exploited the PeopleSoft vulnerability to steal data from dozens of systems across a range of industries, including higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government.

Reuters reported October 5 that the FBI has removed a contractor at Accenture over their failure to patch the FBI recruitment website hacked by ShinyHunters, which exposed sensitive data on more than 5,000 FBI personnel, including each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

According to two sources familiar with the ShinyHunters investigation, a navigation and digital aviation unit recently divested by the global aerospace manufacturer Boeing was among the victims that ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting when Rey was apprehended by Jordanian authorities.

Those sources said the FBI’s investigation into ShinyHunters gained renewed urgency with the group’s attempted extortion of the former Boeing unit, which allegedly included the theft of sensitive information that sources said could pose operational safety and security risks.

In a brief statement shared with KrebsOnSecurity, Boeing acknowledged the extortion attempts by ShinyHunters, and said the incident concerned data stolen from Jeppesen ForeFlight, a subsidiary that Boeing sold in November 2025 to the private equity firm Thoma Bravo for $10.55 billion.

“We are aware of claims by a threat actor regarding data allegedly associated with Boeing and our former subsidiary Jeppesen ForeFlight,” a Boeing spokesperson shared. “We are actively reviewing the matter with the Jeppesen ForeFlight team.”.

A spokesperson for Jeppesen ForeFlight shared a written statement in response to questions, saying the company has seen no impact on their end. “Based on our investigation to date into this claim and proactive security posture, there was no impact to our operations or products.”.

Rey’s alleged involvement in attempting to extort the former Boeing unit is noteworthy because there is strong evidence that his father works for Royal Jordanian Airlines, which is mostly controlled by the Jordanian government and operates its long-haul fleet on passenger planes built by Boeing. Rey claimed on Telegram in early 2025 that his father was an airline pilot, although that could not be independently confirmed.

In a recent development, royal Jordanian Airlines has not yet responded to a request for comment. In advance of our September 28 story, KrebsOnSecurity once again emailed Rey’s father to seek comment and update him on his son’s alleged activities. Neither of the Khaders have responded. But just hours after that request was sent, Rey began deleting his various social media accounts, including the Twitter/X account he previously used to taunt the FBI, Cl0p, and other ShinyHunters victims.

Rey may have nixed many of his social media profiles, but his cybersecurity blog on GitHub somehow escaped the purge, and it reveals that Rey was fixated on the leaders of the Cl0p ransomware group. In March 2026, Rey’s blog featured a lengthy post that identified two Russian men as the core developers and hackers behind Cl0p.

Recent findings suggest that rey’s blog on GitHub. This post doxes two Russian men as the core operators behind Cl0p, one of the oldest and most established ransomware groups still in operation today.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, news outlets in the Netherlands reported explosive new allegations leveled at Van der Stap, whose supposed personal transformation from convicted to reformed hacker has been widely covered in the tech news media. The Dutch daily RTL reported on Sept. 29 that investigators suspect Van der Stap tried to orchestrate at least two murders. According to RTL, the murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for these attacks.

Van der Stap was released from prison after serving the better part of a four year sentence for data theft and extortion activity that prosecutors noted netted between €1.5 million and €2.7 million. In an interview with KrebsOnSecurity on September 9, Van der Stap described his new role as “offensive security lead” at the Dutch cybersecurity company Neo Security, saying the job involved probing client networks for security vulnerabilities.

According to recent reports, neo Security’s owner Benjamin Korper told Reuters he has hired an outside firm to investigate whether Van der Stap had hacked Neo Security or its customers, but that so far investigators have found no evidence he acted against his employer or clients. Korper noted Dutch forensic investigators visited his office on September 15, the night Van der ⁠Stap was arrested in a dramatic police raid that reportedly involved flash bang grenades.

A screenshot of a Sept 16 story by the Dutch news outlet at5.nl, describing a police raid on Van Der Stap’s residence that reportedly used flash-bang grenades.

Prior to his first arrest in 2023, Van der Stap was working as a software engineer at the Amsterdam-based cybersecurity startup Hadrian, while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) — even as he was hacking into and extorting a number of large organizations.

When asked in a recent interview why anyone should believe the word of a self-described “reformed” cybercriminal who had so casually deceived countless friends, co-workers and journalists for years, Van der Stap replied that his work spoke for itself and there was nothing he could say that would convince his worst critics.

Recent findings suggest that “You can throw a bunch of nice words at someone, but you can’t convince them if they don’t want to be convinced,” Van der Stap told KrebsOnSecurity on Sept. 9. “I’m doing what I can to repay victims, and that’s all I can do. If someone doesn’t want to believe me, then that’s on them.”.

Cybercriminals aligned with ShinyHunters have been responsible for dozens of data breaches involving billions of stolen records, and breaches claimed by the group stretch back to at least 2019. But experts say the people recently operating behind the ShinyHunters name are not the same core members that populated the group in its early days, most of whom are French citizens who have been arrested (if not also imprisoned) on at least one prior occasion for alleged cybercrime activity.

In a recent development, more to the point, ShinyHunters has become something of a franchise. Think the Dread Pirate Roberts character in the 1980s cult movie classic “The Princess Bride,” only succession by death is replaced with succession by arrest, and there can be multiple simultaneous Dread Pirate Robertses. Sources close to the investigation say the FBI is focusing on a remaining handful of cybercriminal freelancers or affiliates who have been feeding the group stolen credentials to various software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms used by major companies in exchange for a cut of any data ransoms later paid by victims.

In the days after the news broke of Van der Stap’s arrest, a cybercrime-focused chat server on Telegram that was allegedly operated by Rey erupted with hot takes, with most participants heaping ridicule on the teenage hacker after he publicly backed down from threats against the FBI and Cl0p, and again when the ShinyHunters’s darknet website suddenly went offline. Several commentators accused Rey of resurrecting the ShinyHunters brand after its core members were rounded up in France, and making a mockery of the group’s name and reputation ever since.

“He bought the old forum PGP key and used it to make newly introduced Breachforum websites and Telegram channels larping as ShinyHunters to ransom companies and then sell the used data or resell his forum when he goes broke,” one member recounted.

Recent findings suggest that A relatively fresh Telegram channel called “The Battle” has been doxing and needling Rey and other alleged ShinyHunters members for several weeks, and it has gained a considerable readership among the cybercrime communities operating on Telegram. One of the coordinators of that harassment campaign repeatedly portrayed Rey as clueless greenhorn who sought to ride the coattails of a cybercriminal brand that has long enjoyed a reputation for ruthlessly selling or publishing data stolen from victim companies who refuse to give in to extortion demands.

Recent findings suggest that “Rey (Saif Al-Din Khader) made a serious mistake when he started pretending to be a member of ShinyHunters,” wrote the administrators of The Battle server on Telegram. “That group had already been dismantled, with many of its members either arrested or imprisoned, yet Rey still chose to use its name while carrying out his crimes. We’re aware of claims that [Rey] caused over $200 million in damages and helped around 5–6 friend groups in the community make money by using Shiny Hunters group aliases to negotiate deals for a 25–30% cut over the past few months.”.

In an interview with The Register, ShinyHunters claimed they hacked the FBI to counter the agency’s narrative in a May 2026 alert that advised victims against paying a ransom to the group, which came off looking unprofessional and capricious in the FBI’s advisory.

A flash notice on ShinyHunters released by the FBI on May 15, 2026.

Sources indicate that the public notice warned the group has been known to pursue a number of different victim harassment strategies, from sending threatening text messages and phone calls to victims and their family members to in some cases swatting victims. The FBI warned ShinyHunters members “may also falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist.”.

The hackers told The Register their attack on the FBI “demonstrated our technical capabilities and directly refuted the misinformation disseminated by the FBI, journalists, and industry researchers.” At the same time, the group’s leaders seemed to acknowledge that the FBI’s warning materially harmed their prospects for convincing victims to pay, saying “this was fundamentally a public relations and marketing initiative for our business.”.

According to recent reports, none of these bugs are in the few lines you wrote. All of them arrived with those few lines of CSS.

In a recent development, in my last article on how CSS is growing smarter, I left a few questions hanging at the end, including: What happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, and how do we debug conditional styles without a clear view of what triggered them? This article is my attempt to answer these two questions.

I think it’s worth saying clearly that I am not saying modern CSS is bad. What I am saying is that:.

A CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about if you don’t understand how it relates to existing code, be it CSS or JavaScript.

Think of a latest CSS feature as a new tenant moving into a shared apartment. The tenant may be quiet and tidy, but they still share a kitchen with everyone who already lives there. In that case, CSS is now roommates with JavaScript, the component’s layout, the CSS Cascade, and the browser’s rendering engine. The apartment’s stability depends less on the tenant and more on how they get along with one another.

That gives us two different things to measure, and a diff only indicates the first one:.

I am not the only one thinking about this. In April 2026, Igor Roztropiński published an essay titled “Modern Frontend Complexity: essential or accidental?” asking:.

The essay landed on r/programming, where the thread has drawn 80-plus comments and the replies pull in two directions. One of the most upvoted comments, from a user named Kwantuum, pushes back on the whole genre:.

Another commenter, kayinfire, takes the other side, arguing that “there are tons of scenarios where a front-end framework introduces more accidental complexity than it’s worth.” They say this a few replies later:.

I think both commenters are on to something, and this article lives in the gap between the two. Yes, CSS has improved in the last several years. And yes, “less” CSS on paper is not automatically “less” complexity in practice. That mentioned, my claim is narrower. A native feature only reduces complexity when it actually replaces what was there before and doesn’t disrupt the calm state of everything else it interacts with.

Let’s meet the housemates in our metaphorical apartment, one scenario at a time.

Sources indicate that the first housemate is JavaScript, and the trouble starts when the old tenant never quite moves out. Here is a card that switches to a two-column layout when it has enough room. The original version uses a ResizeObserver to toggle a class:.

With CSS Container Queries, we need no script at all and can simplify our selectors at the same time:.

In a recent development, lovely. Now, here’s the thing: migrations rarely happen in one clean sweep. The pull request adds the @container rule and removes the .card--wide .card__body rule. The observer survives because it is registered in another file. The .card--wide .card__title rule survives because nobody searched for the class. Nothing looks broken, because both implementations agree on 480px. Then a designer asks to move the breakpoint to 600px, and a developer updates the only place they know about: the @container rule.

See the Pen [Scenario 1: The Behaviour With Two Owners [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/ZYeqvpx) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

According to recent reports, between 480px and 600px, the card now has a single-column body and a wide-layout title. Nobody wrote that state. To find it, you need to know that the layout has two owners and read both of them.

The same trap comes in other shapes:.

CSS and JavaScript can happily share a component. What they cannot share is the component’s behavior. So, instead of having a silent fight over a component’s behavior, check first. Know all the contending parties, then split the work.

Industry observers note that and when you’re done migrating, you have to finish the job: delete the observer, the class, and every selector that mentions the class. Otherwise, you may wind up with a tenant who simply refuses to move out.

Back in 2023, I wrote about how block formatting contexts solve float problems. Back then, creating a block formatting context was something we did on purpose. Today, you can create one without meaning to. When we declare container-type: inline-size, we think we are saying, “let my children query my width.” The browser hears quite a bit more. This is the second housemate, the layout around the component, and our upcoming tenant who just asked for one shelf has ended up rearranging the living room.

Sources indicate that according to MDN’s container-type reference, the value “applies style and inline-size containment to the element.” And MDN’s guide to block formatting contexts lists “query containers (elements where container-type isn’t normal)” among the CSS styles that create one. An element that establishes a fresh block formatting context will, in MDN’s words:.

That means one declaration can change three layout behaviors that have nothing to do with queries, plus a fourth that comes from inline-size containment. I built a demo where each “before” and “after” pair differs by only that one declaration.

See the Pen [Scenario 2: The Card That Vanished [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/dPvgJpB) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

A paragraph with margin-bottom: 16px sits above the card, and the card’s heading has margin-top: 24px. Before the change, the heading’s margin collapsed through the top of the card and merged with the paragraph’s margin, leaving a 24px gap. Afterward, the margin remained trapped inside the card. The two margins now add up to 40px, and the card grows from 30px to 54px tall.

Recent findings suggest that the card follows a floated image. Before the change, the card’s box ran behind the float and its text wrapped around the image. Afterward, the whole card sits beside the float; it starts 120px further in (the width of the image) and is 120px narrower.

This is the one that makes cards vanish. Inline-size containment stops an element from taking its width from its contents. MDN has a nice, succinct explanation:.

In the last demo, three tag-sized cards sit in a flex row and measure roughly 74px, 96px, and 114px, respectively. If we add container-type: inline-size, then all three measure 0px. I got the same 0px result when the card was displayed inline-block, floated, set to a width: fit-content box, was an align-items: flex-start child of a column flex container, and when it was an item in an auto grid track. A plain block-level card retains its full width because its width is determined by its parent rather than its contents.

In isolation, the card is a block that fills its parent. In reality, it is a flex item, follows a float, or sits under a paragraph whose margin it used to absorb.

Answering these will help prevent a housemate from completely changing the furniture layout right from under you.

According to recent reports, the third housemate is the CSS Cascade. Every shared apartment has house rules about who gets the last word, and a newly introduced tenant can arrive with more say than anyone expected.

The :has() selector and native nesting let us write short selectors in CSS. But short selectors can match more and weigh more than they appear.

The body text of the card above it loses its spacing. Good luck reproducing that from a bug report that notes “spacing looks off sometimes.”.

This helps the selector get more specific about what it is yelling about.

Industry observers note that native nesting has the same habit. MDN’s guide to nesting and specificity indicates the & selector takes “the largest specificity in the associated selector list,” exactly like :is(). Look at this adaptation of MDN’s example:.

A .button link inside a .card is blue, even though the #featured ID is nowhere near it. The usual reaction is a more specific .button rule, then an exception to that rule. Before you know it, you are in a war of specificity you never knew you had declared.

The way out is to keep the selector list and drop its weight by wrapping it in :where():.

Plain links inside a card are still blue, and the .button link is red again. Again, another way to quiet the loud housemate.

It has been revealed that don’t be fooled into thinking specificity is the whole story. MDN’s introduction to the cascade puts origin, importance, and cascade layers ahead of specificity, and notes that “normal layered styles have less precedence than normal unlayered styles.” In my test, a layered rule with a specificity of 0-4-0 lost to an unlayered .title (0-1-0). So if your new component styles go into @layer components while the legacy stylesheet stays unlayered, the legacy rule wins every conflict, however carefully you wrote the new one. The exception is when the !vital keyword is used, because it actually reverses the cascade order.

Sources indicate that miriam Suzanne’s original proposal for cascade layers describes exactly the pain layers were meant to remove: having to “be very careful with matching specificity to layer.” Layers do remove it, but only when the rules on both sides of the conflict are layered. A half-layered codebase just gives you one more ordering to keep in your head.

None of these battles started with :has() or nesting. In an r/webdev thread titled “CSS-in-JS: What’s the biggest performance drop you actually felt?”, one of the most upvoted answers isn’t about performance at all. It is about the cascade:.

This is about the “order of appearance,” which is the last step in the cascade that ends up deciding a conflict nobody knew existed. Another commenter in the subreddit adds that the injected styles can land in a different order in development and production builds: “Who doesn’t love debugging something that works locally but not in prod.”.

Not everyone in the thread agrees on who is to blame. TheThirdRace replies, “It’s a coding matter, not a technology issue.”.

I think both are right, and that is exactly the point. CSS-in-JS is a different technology from the native features we are looking at, so take this as a neighboring example, not as proof. But the shape of the problem is the same: the tool did what it promised, and the trouble arose from how it complied with the existing rules.

In a recent development, “We moved it to CSS, so it’s faster now.” You have probably heard this in a code review, and maybe said it yourself. In my last article, I warned that it isn’t always the case. Let’s test it.

It has been revealed that moving a behavior from JavaScript to CSS changes who does the work. It doesn’t tell you how much work there is. The last housemate, the browser’s rendering engine, is the one who gets the bill. Everyone in the apartment shares it, and nobody looks at it after the move.

Take :has() as an example. Browser vendors were worried about its cost from the start. In a CSS Working Group glitch about :has() restrictions, Emilio Cobos Álvarez noted that implementations wanted to ship it with limitations “in order to prevent performance footguns and complexity.” Today, MDN’s :has() page has a whole section on performance with two pieces of advice:.

It has been revealed that I wanted numbers, so I built a list with 5,000 rows. The test toggles an .is-selected class on the same row 300 times, so the row’s selected state changes on every toggle, and forces a style and layout update each time. I ran it in Chrome 153 on a Mac in October 2026, and recorded a trace in DevTools to count how many elements each toggle restyles.

See the Pen [Scenario 4: The Rewrite Nobody Measured [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVgP) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

There are two lessons in that table.

First, the “bad” selector was fine. Rule 2 is exactly the shape MDN warns against: a :has() anchored to body. It cost about a millisecond and a half more than the script, and it restyled a single element, the toolbar. A frame at 60Hz lasts 16.7ms, so I would take that trade for deleting an event handler any day.

According to recent reports, second, two harmless rules were not harmless together. Rule 3 styles the rows, and its :has() condition remains unchanged throughout the test. On its own, it costs nothing measurable. Put it in the same stylesheet as the second rule instead, and every toggle restyles all 5,000 rows plus the toolbar. That is about what it costs a script to restyle every row on purpose.

Sources indicate that let’s keep this in proportion. Since 7ms still fits inside a frame, nobody would notice it on this page. However, the browser is now restyling 5,001 elements to change just one, and neither rule notes so. Also, the cost grows with the list. When I set the demo to 20,000 rows, the two rules together restyled 20,001 elements and took about 31ms per toggle, which is nearly two frames.

Sources indicate that I can tell you what Chrome does here, but not why. Changing .is-selected on one row restyles every element that the other :has() rule targets, even though that rule never mentions .is-selected and its result never changes. I have filed this with the Chromium team as an matter, with a reduced test case, and I only tested Chrome. Whatever the cause, neither rule looks suspicious in a code review, and the cost applies only when both are met.

It has been revealed that that is system complexity in a single table. And please take the pattern from it, not the numbers: this is one page, one browser, and one machine.

The same goes for animation. The animation guide on web.dev recommends restricting animations to opacity and transform where possible, and warns that “an animation that moves an element using something other than transform is likely to be slow.” MDN’s CSS performance guide lists the properties that trigger layout when animated, such as width, height, margin, top, and left. A CSS transition on left runs layout on every frame, while a JavaScript animation of transform skips it. The property determines the cost, regardless of which language you write it in.

According to recent reports, to be fair, CSS often wins. A script that reads layout, writes styles, and reads layout again forces the browser to do layout several times in one frame, and a container query hands that whole job to the browser. But that win is something you can measure, so measure it:.

Each of these scenarios is small on its own. The trouble is that a real migration could hit all four scenarios at once. You have already seen three of them. They are the three bugs in the “after” demo at the top of this article. Add a long list, and you get the fourth. One move-in, four housemates disturbed.

It has been revealed that A team replaces a card’s JavaScript-driven responsive layout with a container query and :has(). The pull request adds twelve lines of CSS, deletes one script, and misses another. Within a month, three bug reports land, and there’s a chance a performance trace turns up as the fourth problem:.

According to recent reports, none of these reports means that container queries or :has() were the wrong choice. Each bug lives in the meeting point between the new CSS and the system it moved into. Still, one small pull request has sent a developer through the JavaScript, the page layout, the cascade, and the profiler.

And the way out is not a return to JavaScript. Here is the same page once more, fixed.

See the Pen [demo (fixed PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/wBJYpPJ) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

It still uses a container query and :has(), with three changes:.

It has been revealed that this gap between a clean start and a real codebase shows up in the same r/webdev thread. The person who started it, JRM_Insights, opens with an observation that could describe any of our four scenarios:.

Further down, mq2thez describes moving an old CSS-in-JS codebase to a newer pattern: “In isolation or greenfield maybe it wouldn’t be a huge glitch,” but in practice, it meant rewriting “whole component trees.” TheThirdRace, who had been defending the technology, answers that they had only ever evaluated it “from a greenfield project perspective,” and that it was “very enlightening to see this through the lens of a spaghetti CSS migration.”.

That is the honest version of this whole article.

Industry observers note that most of what we read about a new feature is written from the greenfield perspective. Most of what we ship is a migration.

Sources indicate that before you replace JavaScript with a modern CSS feature, or adopt one in an existing codebase, answer these six questions. Think of them as the conversation to have with the housemates before the fresh tenant gets a key. I suggest putting the answers right in the pull request description.

Modern CSS is great and a huge improvement to styling as a whole. In particular, container queries and :has() let us express things that used to need a script, a dependency, or a hack. But a new capability does not hand us a simpler system by default. In every scenario we looked at, the new tenant did something that didn’t sit well with others, and that was because nobody introduced them to the housemates’ ways of doing things. We get a simpler system when the new rule has one clear owner, a scope we have checked, a place in the cascade we chose on purpose, and numbers showing it helped.

So, the next time a pull request deletes more than it adds, enjoy the red lines. Then ask where the complexity went, and run the six questions. If you can’t answer one of them, the migration isn’t finished yet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Three Trezor Safe 5 wallets bought from the reseller CryptoBilis contain an implant, an extra circuit board that can copy their recovery phrases, hardware wallet maker Trezor remarked yesterday.

It has been revealed that the implant reads the phrase from the wallet's screen and sends it over the mobile network to a server controlled by the attackers. The company examined one of the wallets in its lab, identified the other two from photos their owners sent, and has had no reports of lost funds.

A firmware revision released earlier this week, version 2.13.1, stops the implants found so far from capturing anything on wallets that run it, the organization stated, but “the update can’t protect a wallet backup that was captured before it.”.

The company has not changed its advice to anyone who bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis since March, including from the reseller's stores on Tokopedia and Shopee:.

Version 2.13.1 was released for the Safe 7, Safe 5, Safe 3 and Model T, according to the organization's firmware changelog. The company will not publish technical details that could help attackers or put customers at risk, it said in an investigation enhancement.

Its engineers extracted and analyzed the implant's firmware from the first wallet it reported. The implant sits between the Safe 5's main board and its screen and changes nothing on the wallet itself, including its firmware and Secure Element, the manufacturer found.

The implant copies the recovery phrase when the wallet reveals it during backup creation, and when someone types it in to restore an existing wallet to the device. It also copies a passphrase if one appears on the screen. It encrypts the data before sending it, and if it cannot connect, it keeps the data and tries again until it succeeds.

The company first warned of a suspected implant on October 30, two days after a buyer reported it and before its lab had seen the wallet.

Industry observers note that cryptoBilis served as an official reseller for the company's wallets in Southeast Asia until October 9, when the company removed it. That was the day Ledger, another hardware wallet maker, began investigating losses of funds among the reseller's customers.

Ledger later confirmed an unauthorized implant in a wallet the reseller sold. Attackers had fitted genuine Ledger devices with hidden components designed to capture the recovery phrase during setup, then drained wallets in a single coordinated operation, Ledger remarked in an incident statement.

Industry observers note that trezor says the implants in its wallets work the same way as those found in Ledger devices, adapted to the Safe 5's display. It has not stated who fitted the implants or where in the supply chain that happened.

The three wallets were bought between August 20 and September 23. So far the company has found implants only in Safe 5 wallets sold by the reseller, and none in wallets from its other resellers or in its other models.

In a recent development, after the October reports, it asked people who bought a Trezor from the reseller to get in touch, and 48 have done so. It is checking their wallets in its lab or from photos of the insides, and has not said how many it has checked so far.

Industry observers note that the manufacturer says none of the three owners has lost funds. Trezor wallets are self-custodial, so it cannot see anyone's balance.

In a recent development, the organization notes it has cut its reseller network by about 80%, dropping trustworthy partners that posed no immediate threat but did not fit its stricter newly introduced rules. It first unveiled the reduction on October 13 in a post on X, more than two weeks before the first report of an implant in one of its own wallets.

In a partner letter that day, it told the dropped resellers that they would get no fresh stock, could sell what they had until January 1, 2027, and would then be removed from its list of authorized sellers.

Sources indicate that it is still investigating. It will post an update if it confirms an implant outside the reseller's wallets or the Safe 5, receives a report of lost funds linked to the implants, or releases latest protections.

Making Interrupted AI Streams Visible: A React 19 SSE Implementation

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, an AI assistant stops mid-sentence.
  • For IDE integrations around agentic systems like JetBrains/thinkrail, the missing distinction between "finished," "cancelled," and "connection lost" creates authorization risks.
  • React 19 client → Next.js route → OpenAI-compatible relay → model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, an AI assistant stops mid-sentence. Your UI demonstrates "complete." The user clicks Approve, and the partial instruction deletes the wrong database table. The postmortem reveals a dropped connection two seconds before the actual termination token arrived. This is not hypothetical.

For IDE integrations around agentic systems like JetBrains/thinkrail, the missing distinction between "finished," "cancelled," and "connection lost" creates authorization risks. Partial output cannot safely trigger edits or imply that an agent action succeeded. This article presents a companion chat integration pattern that preserves honest UI state when assistant streams are interrupted.

React 19 client → Next.js route → OpenAI-compatible relay → model.

In a recent development, the client speaks the Vercel AI SDK's UI message stream protocol. The upstream relay speaks OpenAI-compatible streaming. Those are not interchangeable despite both traveling over SSE. The server performs translation through streamText() and toUIMessageStreamResponse(). Returning raw upstream bytes to useChat() produces parser failures—the client expects SDK-specific message events, not arbitrary delta objects.

Sources indicate that the browser owns rendering and user cancellation. The route owns credentials, model selection, protocol translation, and upstream cancellation. Neither component pretends reconnecting resumes an existing generation.

Start inside an existing React 19 Next.js App Router application. This block installs dependencies, writes the route and page, and creates the environment template. Replace both environment values before starting the development server.

This is a runnable transport baseline. Add session validation, request-size limits, and message sanitization before accepting external traffic.

It has been revealed that clicking Stop cancels the client request. Passing req.signal upstream propagates that cancellation when the hosting adapter exposes disconnects correctly. This is not universal—a reverse proxy may keep the server-side request alive after the browser disconnects. Test cancellation through deployed ingress, not only against localhost.

According to recent reports, similarly, X-Accel-Buffering: no works for compatible Nginx configurations but cannot override every CDN buffering policy. If tokens arrive in one burst, compare upstream timestamps with browser timestamps to separate model latency from intermediary buffering.

Sources indicate that the 50-millisecond render throttle reduces React patch pressure during token bursts. It does not slow generation or repair blocked streams. Avoid reparsing entire growing Markdown documents on every token—rendering cost can make healthy connections appear frozen.

In a recent development, maxRetries: 0 makes the retry policy explicit. After visible output exists, silently launching another generation can duplicate text or produce a different answer. A resumed HTTP connection is not a resumed model execution.

Recent findings suggest that the baseline retains partial output and labels detected failures. It does not provide durable stream resumption. A cleanly closed but semantically incomplete response may escape ordinary transport error detection. Stronger guarantees require persisted generation identifiers and explicit terminal-state reconciliation.

Recent findings suggest that for IDE integrations, this limitation matters: incomplete assistant text must not authorize an edit. Keep action results separate from conversational progress. Require a confirmed terminal result before presenting work as complete.

The hardest operational question: When do you trust a stream enough to execute its instructions? The baseline above preserves failure signals but cannot prove semantic completeness. How do you reconcile streaming UX with the requirement that partial output never triggers destructive actions? What patterns have held up in your production agent integrations?

Edward Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile.

Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations.
