  • Recent findings suggest that the source contained a 600 × 420 board, two native Inter text objects, a fixed 400 × 80 horizontal auto-layout row with 12 px padding and a 16 px gap, two 120 × 40 rectangles, and a simple 100 × 48 component with a linked instance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ten objects went into a small Figma migration fixture, and ten came out in Penpot. That count was a useful first check. It did not tell us whether text stayed editable, a component instance still followed its source, or the layout behaved after resizing.

Recent findings suggest that this note describes one recorded test from November 13, 2026. It uses a deliberately small fixture and reports the differences as well as the successful checks. It is not a general compatibility verdict.

Recent findings suggest that the source contained a 600 × 420 board, two native Inter text objects, a fixed 400 × 80 horizontal auto-layout row with 12 px padding and a 16 px gap, two 120 × 40 rectangles, and a simple 100 × 48 component with a linked instance. There were ten non-root objects and one component definition.

According to recent reports, the fixture was created through the Figma plugin API. Its properties and component links were read back before export. Penpot Exporter v0.26.3 then exported all pages to a .penpot archive of 13,699 bytes. The archive was imported through Penpot's cloud interface and opened as a separate copy.

This was an exporter-to-native-archive workflow. It did not test opening a .fig file directly in Penpot.

Industry observers note that the horizontal Figma row became a Penpot Flex layout with row-reverse. The child order also reversed.

It has been revealed that reading only the direction field would make this look like an immediate ordering failure. The measured positions told a different story: rectangle A remained at (36, 132), rectangle B at (172, 132), and both stayed 120 × 40. The horizontal gap was still:.

It has been revealed that the visible order and spacing survived this conversion. The underlying layout representation changed.

A separate behavior check widened the fixed row from 400 to approximately 480 through the Penpot plugin API. The two fixed-size rectangles kept their recorded positions, dimensions and gap; the row was then restored to 400. This covers one fixed row. It says nothing about nested layouts, fill or hug sizing.

Both strings remained native text objects. Inter, weight 400 and the two recorded font sizes, 28 and 16, were retained. Their bounds changed:.

Industry observers note that to check editing, the heading was temporarily changed through the Penpot plugin API. Its width changed to 412, after which the original text was restored. That establishes an actual edit in this fixture, rather than just the presence of a text string in an exported structure.

Recent findings suggest that the dimension differences also mean this was not a pixel-identical migration. Other fonts, mixed styles and CJK text were outside the test.

The imported main object and instance pointed to the same component definition. A temporary change to the main rectangle's fill, from #1A66B2 to #2D8C51, propagated to the instance. Restoring the original fill propagated as well.

Sources indicate that this tested one same-file rectangle fill. It did not cover variants, overrides, cross-file libraries or design tokens.

After reloading the Penpot file, a further read-back confirmed the ten objects, original strings, restored 400 px row, 16 px gap, original color and component links.

According to recent reports, the Penpot MCP export_shape request for a PNG preview returned HTTP 500 / ResourceRequest timeout. The design was visible in the browser, and editor screenshots were saved, but those screenshots do not establish that server-side PNG export worked.

Recent findings suggest that the native archive import and the preview export are separate operations. The first succeeded in this fixture; the second failed. The failure's cause was not established.

It has been revealed that start with a copy containing a few features you depend on. Record source counts, text, dimensions, positions and component relationships. Export and import through the documented route, then inspect both the structure and visible geometry.

Next, make a reversible edit: change text, resize a layout container or change a component property. Check the result, restore the original state, reload, and check again. Test image export separately from import.

This fixture did not cover complex components, prototypes, collaboration, self-hosting, large production files or other versions. A successful small-file check is a starting point for deciding what to test next.

Sources indicate that the experiment was recorded for FOSS Desk, which I maintain. The Figma-to-Penpot guide includes these scoped results and their limits. The separate public software list and read-only release checker covers release metadata; it does not contain this migration fixture or its private evidence archive.

AI assistance was used to organize and draft this article from recorded project evidence. The experiment's results and limitations are identified above.

#29. Tech Report: Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1682 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Css-tricks

Tech Report: Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites, the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages.
  • When CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier.
  • Industry observers note that twelve-column grids weren’t invented in the 2000s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites, the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages. CSS eventually gave us more control over layouts through floats and positioning. Neither was intended for page layout, and inconsistent browser behaviour could make using them frustrating. Still, that didn’t stop me and a generation of other designers from using floats and positioning.

When CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier. Blueprint CSS) offered a 24-column grid, while Nathan Smith’s 960 Grid System offered 12- and 16-column options. These frameworks gave designers and developers a shared structure, making layout planning and implementation considerably easier.

Industry observers note that twelve-column grids weren’t invented in the 2000s. Graphic designers had used column-based and modular grids for decades, and twelve is a convenient number because you don’t need to be a maths genius to divide it into halves, thirds, and quarters to create the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up components we see everywhere online.

It has been revealed that frameworks like Bootstrap and Foundation followed, helping establish twelve-column grids as the de facto standard for page layouts. I get why that happened. But somewhere along the way, one layout option became the default starting point for almost everything.

CSS Grid changed what’s possible for page layouts, but I still see designers start by dividing a page into twelve equal columns, then deciding how to fit their content into them. The designs they end up with might be perfectly fine, but they can also look remarkably similar.

Recent findings suggest that still, I don’t think twelve-column grids themselves are the problem. It’s reaching for a familiar solution before considering what makes the organization I’m designing for distinctive and what its website needs to communicate. So what happens when I start with those questions instead?

In a recent development, before I decide how many columns a layout needs, I want to understand the manufacturer I’m designing for. What makes it different from its competitors? What does it want people to remember? Does it have a personality that could influence how its website looks and feels?

These questions matter because a layout does more than arrange content. The size, position, and relationships between elements influence how people experience a website. A restrained, orderly composition can communicate something very different from one that’s full of energy and movement. So to demonstrate what I mean, I’ll use Wheelman. It’s a fictional company I invented for my book, Standout Designs for the Web.

Pre-orders for Standout Designs for the Web are now open in the CSS-Tricks store.

Industry observers note that wheelman provides products and services for getaway drivers, including legal advice, robbery insurance, and an online shop selling break-in essentials. It also publishes a magazine with advice, news, and stories about life behind the wheel.

Wheelman isn’t an ordinary tech giant, so why should its website look like an everyday collection of components? It takes its business seriously, but isn’t afraid to have fun with its design. It’s rebellious, but doesn’t want to look off-putting. Its audience is criminals, but they demand professionalism. Wheelman has plenty of personality to work with, and I want its designs to reflect that.

Recent findings suggest that that doesn’t mean making Wheelman different for difference’s sake. Its customers still need to find what they’re looking for, understand what it provides, and buy its products and services. But I can make those experiences more memorable by choosing layouts that fit the company, rather than settling for familiar arrangements.

It has been revealed that let’s imagine I’m designing a upcoming landing page for Wheelman’s online shop. It includes two products, one with a gigantic headline, product images, and the type of functionality and information you’ll find on most stores.

Recent findings suggest that before I decide how to arrange these elements, I want to look beyond them and consider how they relate. I ask myself questions like:.

Industry observers note that only then do I start thinking about visual design questions: “Would a large photograph set the scene? Should I make the introduction more prominent? Can whitespace lead the eye and create spaces to pause? How can I bring images and text together into a considered composition?”.

These questions help me understand what the layout needs to accomplish before I decide which grid might help me achieve it.

I could arrange everything in a single column for a straightforward reading experience. That would make responsive design considerably easier. But I won’t.

According to recent reports, wheelman has a rebellious personality, and I want its shop to reflect that. A more energetic layout seems appropriate, but I still need to establish a clear hierarchy between the products and their information. Two equal-width columns give both products equal prominence.

Changing their proportions creates a hierarchy, even when most elements stay the same size.

I could base those proportions on a twelve-column grid, but I won’t. Columns only divide space vertically, and I want a layout that adds another dimension.

Dividing a layout into columns is a useful starting point, but adding rows creates another dimension and opens up more creative possibilities. Where columns and rows intersect, they form rectangular or square units called modules.

Combining these modules creates larger spatial zones that can establish hierarchy, control whitespace, and add variety to a composition.

Sources indicate that using a modular grid, I can add drama, establish hierarchy by varying scale, and make the composition feel far less predictable. Starting with four columns and four rows gives me sixteen modules to work with, but I don’t need to fill them all.

I can create drama by spreading the large graphic headline and product image across four modules, while the product information and shopping tools occupy one module each.

The modular structure becomes even more apparent in the grid of alternative products. Most occupy just one module, while others fill two, either horizontally or vertically. Varying their sizes gives some products more prominence and makes the overall arrangement feel less predictable.

In a recent development, the result still feels like a product page, with a clear reading order and space for the content to breathe. But it also feels unmistakably like something Wheelman would publish.

I don’t expect this composition to work at every screen size, so I can adjust the size and quantity of modules to improve the reading experience.

And if one grid offers this much flexibility, imagine what combining two or more grids can do.

In a recent development, one thing I want from Wheelman’s website is variety. Its magazine, shop, and services serve different purposes, and I don’t want every page to feel like I’ve poured its content into the same template.

It has been revealed that wheelman needs layouts which feel organised without being predictable. Compound grids give me the structure I need while leaving room for less conventional arrangements.

In a recent development, A compound grid combines two or more grids of any type — column, modular, or hierarchical — on the same page. These grids can overlap, sit side by side, or be stacked one on top of the other. Combining grids creates possibilities which neither grid offers on its own.

Industry observers note that I can start by overlaying a two-column grid with one containing three columns. Their combined grid lines create four columns of two different widths, giving me more flexibility without losing the underlying structure.

Those proportions offer more possibilities for arranging content. I might use a wider area for a photograph or headline, then place a pullquote into one of the narrower spaces. Another page could use the same underlying grid but combine its spaces differently to suit another story.

Recent findings suggest that combining grids with different column counts gets even more interesting as those numbers increase. In Standout Designs for the Web, I explore several combinations, including mixing four- and five-column grids to create different compositions for Wheelman’s pages while maintaining a connected visual structure.

It has been revealed that the point isn’t to make every page look different for its own sake. It’s to give each section a layout that suits its content while keeping them all feeling like part of the same firm.

It has been revealed that twelve-column grids are useful, and I’m certainly not suggesting you should stop using them entirely. But they’re only one option among many, and starting every design with the same structure limits your possibilities before you’ve even considered the story your design is telling.

There’s also nothing inherently wrong with the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up patterns a twelve-column grid inspires. They can sometimes be exactly what’s needed. But reaching for them automatically can leave little room for the character and personality that make websites memorable.

Recent findings suggest that wheelman gives me plenty of reasons to choose different layouts. Its stories, products, and services don’t all need the same arrangements, and its personality gives me opportunities to make those arrangements more distinctive. The grids are simply tools that help me put those ideas into practice.

Industry observers note that and this applies to much more than layout. The same thinking should influence the colours I choose, the typography I use, the images I commission, and the way I bring those elements together.

That’s why I wrote Standout Designs for the Web. I want to encourage designers to look beyond familiar solutions and make more deliberate decisions about colour, typography, imagery, and layout. Not to be different for difference’s sake, but to create websites that look and feel like they belong to the companies behind them. And no one else.

In a recent development, pre-orders for Standout Designs for the Web are open! Everyone who pre-orders will also receive the Hardboiled Client Interview Guide for free — a practical companion to help designers ask better questions and discover what makes a company distinctive.

The book will be published on November 20, priced at $14.99 for the DRM-free EPUB and PDF editions.

Latest Update: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that google noted today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud.
  • A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) stated Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
  • Recent findings suggest that the global distribution of XCPE botnet infections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that google noted today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) stated Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

Recent findings suggest that the global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report stated the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

Sources indicate that “Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”.

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google stated it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm customers, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google indicates it has since addressed that weakness).

According to recent reports, the GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

In a recent development, another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy tech giant operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

It has been revealed that google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box customers.

Industry observers note that synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

Recent findings suggest that in a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

According to recent reports, the MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”.

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”.

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”.

It has been revealed that update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

In a recent development, “We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”.

The statement mentioned Oxylabs has no record of any firm called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that customers had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”.

Cursor Notes Stolen Fireworks AI Key Led to Trojanized Claude Code Extension Incident

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The compromise of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension on Cursor's extension marketplace was the result of the theft of an access key that was exposed in the wake of a breach targeting Fireworks AI.
  • "An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor stated in a Friday upgrade.
  • The disclosure comes nearly two weeks after a trojanized version of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension was distributed through Cursor Marketplace as a legitimate enhancement, attempting to install a persistent SSH backdoor on affected systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The compromise of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension on Cursor's extension marketplace was the result of the theft of an access key that was exposed in the wake of a breach targeting Fireworks AI.

"An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor stated in a Friday upgrade. "The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them.".

The disclosure comes nearly two weeks after a trojanized version of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension was distributed through Cursor Marketplace as a legitimate enhancement, attempting to install a persistent SSH backdoor on affected systems.

According to recent reports, according to the artificial intelligence (AI)-powered coding platform, the read-only storage bucket is noted to have contained limited coding agent traces from sessions that were not in Privacy Mode. Privacy Mode is a Cursor-specific setting that, if enabled, allows consumers to opt out of their data being used for training purposes.

These sessions, most of which date back to 2025, were permitted to be used for model training. Among these traces were credentials that had not been edited out, exposing the API credentials of less than 0.01% of customers in the process.

The attacker, Cursor added, used these credentials as a starting point to reach select software-as-a-service (SaaS) tools used by Cursor and then access the following data -.

Cursor stated it took steps to deactivate the vendor's key, revoke and rotate credentials, and hunt for signs of deeper access, and contain it after "we identified further access." The manufacturer also said it temporarily disabled internal and product services, disrupting access to some Cursor features.

The next phase of the attack took place on October 29, 2026, when the attacker used a stolen credential from the exposed data of its internal system to place trojanized versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension directly on the cache used to serve Cursor's extension marketplace.

Sources indicate that "At most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions of the extension on October 29 potentially received the malicious build," Cursor said. "It was available for approximately 11 hours before we removed it. We took it down, took the extension marketplace offline, and worked with the cloud service provider hosting the attacker's server to take it down.".

Recent findings suggest that the company mentioned it notified affected consumers who installed versions 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 from the marketplace during the exposure window and helped revoke exposed credentials. It has also moved all inference traffic off Fireworks, deactivated the key issued to it, and cut off its access to all data sets we shared with it.

Furthermore, Cursor emphasized that no additional malicious activity has been detected since November 1, 2026.

There is no evidence that the incident impacted customers who had enabled Privacy Mode, customer code repositories, Cursor's own production environment, Cursor app and its official updates, its other apps, or any other extension or plugin downloaded from Cursor Marketplace.

The development comes as Uber confirmed unknown threat actors stole thousands of drivers' license information after obtaining internal credentials.

"On October 9, 2026, a service provider notified Uber that an unauthorized third-party had compromised the service provider's internal credentials and used them to access Uber's account with the service provider," the firm said in a filing with the U.S. state of California. "On October 13, 2026, our investigation determined that the unauthorized party had used the compromised credentials to access Uber data connected to the service provider.".

Although the name of the provider was not disclosed, TechCrunch reported that the provider in question is Fireworks AI. Uber has not disclosed how many owners were impacted by the breach. Last week, online productivity startup Notion also confirmed its data was stolen in the Fireworks AI hack.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A React Native or Expo app feels like a native binary. Owners install it from a store, open an icon, and never see a browser tab. The business logic you wrote in JavaScript or TypeScript still ships as a bundle inside that binary — or as Hermes bytecode that tools can unpack — and an interested person can pull it out of the APK, the IPA, or an OTA upgrade.

This article is about what actually gets packaged, why "it's a mobile app" is not protection, and how to raise the cost of copying the proprietary part.

A conventional release contains:.

Sources indicate that hermes bytecode raises the cost relative to a pretty-printed Metro bundle. It does not encrypt your algorithm. Public and commercial tooling exists to disassemble .hbc, and the strings, API paths, and structure of the program are usually recoverable. An OTA update that you ship as a plain JS bundle for speed can be an easier copy than the store binary you thought was the only artifact.

Expo and React Native Web targets make this even more direct: the same modules may also be on a public URL.

It has been revealed that you do not need a jailbreak to look at your own (or a public) Android package. Anyone can download the APK, unzip it, and search it. iOS IPAs from a device you control, or from TestFlight artifacts you retained in CI, have the same property. Treat those outputs the way you would treat a web dist/ folder.

Minification and Hermes compilation will rename solveOfflineLicense. They will not remove the need for that logic to exist on the device if the feature works offline.

Move off the device when you can:.

Industry observers note that client-side checks are UX and a first filter. They are not the authority. That is the same rule as a web app; the store binary does not change it.

OTA channels need the same hygiene as web previews: do not push an unprotected debug bundle to a public upgrade channel "just for QA," and do not leave old update IDs fetchable after you start protecting production updates.

Sources indicate that some logic genuinely has to be local: an offline preview, a game rule module, a mapper that works in airplane mode. For those:.

A JS VM obfuscator compiles that function to a custom bytecode and ships a small interpreter. The app still runs on the device. A recovered bundle no longer contains the original function in plain JavaScript. It is slower, so do not wrap the UI tree or the animation loop.

According to recent reports, VEILVM is a browser-based JSVMP workspace you can point at one extracted function before you wire protection into the release pipeline. Protection raises the cost of lifting your offline engine out of the APK or an OTA revision. It does not make the store binary opaque, and it does not replace server-side entitlements.

If you want to try VM protection on a single extracted function, VEILVM runs in the browser with no sign-up: 3 free runs a day, up to 5 KB per file (resets at 00:00 UTC). A free account raises the input limit to 30 KB. Pro is $9/month or $79/year and adds an API so the protection step can run in CI. Standard requests are processed in memory and are not written to logs. Start at https://vm.ldvmp.com.

#18. Tech Report: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (774 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Krebsonsecurity

Tech Report: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today.
  • In a recent development, the security firm Layer3 Intel mentioned it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650).
  • The proxy tracking organization Synthient noted on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

In a recent development, the security firm Layer3 Intel mentioned it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 indicated they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking organization Synthient noted on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Sources indicate that synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

Sources indicate that there are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel noted the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

Sources indicate that they can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”.

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox mentioned it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

#15. Italy Fines Meta €805 Million Over Facebook's Android Gallery Access Without Explicit Consent

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (625 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thehackernews

Italy Fines Meta €805 Million Over Facebook's Android Gallery Access Without Explicit Consent

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thehackernews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meta was fined €805 million in Italy yesterday over a Facebook for Android feature that suggests photos and videos from consumers' phone galleries for them to post.
  • The Garante, Italy's data protection authority, found that the feature was enabled by default and that the app accessed Italian consumers' photos, videos, and related metadata without their explicit consent.
  • The tech giant has 60 days to switch the feature off by default, including for people who have already granted the app gallery access, and to request consent separately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta was fined €805 million in Italy yesterday over a Facebook for Android feature that suggests photos and videos from consumers' phone galleries for them to post.

The Garante, Italy's data protection authority, found that the feature was enabled by default and that the app accessed Italian consumers' photos, videos, and related metadata without their explicit consent.

The tech giant has 60 days to switch the feature off by default, including for people who have already granted the app gallery access, and to request consent separately.

Meta prepares to appeal and calls the fine "disproportionate", a spokesperson mentioned in a statement reported by Reuters.

The app asks for gallery access via a single permission that covers the whole app and several functions with different purposes, the authority found. A general notice about enabling other features appears first, but it does not make it clear to users that they are also enabling gallery suggestions.

Fully granted, a permission like this lets the app read the phone's whole photo archive, usually on an ongoing basis. Neither the user nor the authority can check which information is actually used.

The authority found a breach of Article 122 of Italy's Privacy Code, which puts the EU's ePrivacy Directive into Italian law. That rule treats a phone as part of a person's private life. Any access to what the phone stores, therefore, requires free and informed consent, whether or not data is sent anywhere or harm results.

The authority's order, set out in its press release, requires the manufacturer to:.

If the tech giant misses the 60-day deadline, the feature cannot be switched on for anyone who has not given valid consent.

Meta noted in a statement quoted in a Reuters report that the feature works only after users give permission on their device, and that they can change that permission at any time in their settings.

Recent findings suggest that the Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti, the Bolzano consumer protection group whose complaint started the investigation, published consumer advice on July 11, 2025. It told people to switch off the gallery suggestion settings in the app and to check what access and permissions the Facebook app has on their phone.

The investigation did not look at whether gallery content was used to train AI models. The firm denies any such use. The authority may separately examine a newer feature, introduced this year, that allows gallery content to be processed in the cloud.

Sources indicate that the tech giant had argued that Ireland's data protection authority should handle the case. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules do not provide a one-stop-shop mechanism.

Sources indicate that the feature has been available since 2023. The investigation began in July 2025 and included the authority's own technical analysis.

Sources indicate that the fine equals about 0.47% of the group's global revenue. In setting it, the authority weighed the large number of people involved, about 20 million Android users in Italy.

It also weighed how long the breach has lasted. The breach is still ongoing for people who have not updated the app, and for those who have already granted permission, the authority remarked.

Other factors were a 2019 decision against the company and limited cooperation during the investigation. Changes the company made after the complaint counted in its favor, though the authority judged them late and limited to people who update the app.

Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software.
  • Sources indicate that november’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users.
  • According to recent reports, this latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid crucial security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

Sources indicate that november’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

According to recent reports, this latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

It has been revealed that according to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best initiative often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”.

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A fresh version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Sources indicate that chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, mentioned it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

Sources indicate that “Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close rapidly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”.

Please don’t neglect to back up any crucial data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

#8. Breaking: Base64 vs Hex, Base32 and ASCII85: Encodings Compared

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1109 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

Breaking: Base64 vs Hex, Base32 and ASCII85: Encodings Compared

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that base64 is the default choice for turning bytes into text, but it is not the only one and it is not always the right one.
  • The overhead figures are arithmetic, not preference.
  • It has been revealed that hex is the least efficient encoding here and the most useful one when a person is going to look at the data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that base64 is the default choice for turning bytes into text, but it is not the only one and it is not always the right one. Hexadecimal is easier to read and worse at everything else. Base32 is bigger and survives environments that destroy case. ASCII85 is smaller and appears in places you would not expect. Each exists because of a specific constraint, and picking the wrong one is usually a decision nobody made on purpose.

The overhead figures are arithmetic, not preference. Hex spends exactly two characters per byte, so it doubles the data. Base32 packs 5 bits per character, so it needs 8 characters to carry the 40 bits of 5 bytes — 60% overhead. Base64 packs 6 bits into 4 characters for 3 bytes. ASCII85 packs 4 bytes into 5 characters, the most efficient of the four; it is what PostScript and PDF use for embedded streams.

It has been revealed that hex is the least efficient encoding here and the most useful one when a person is going to look at the data. Every byte maps to a fixed pair of characters, so the mapping is memorisable and offsets are trivially readable: byte 4 of a file is characters 8 and 9 in the hex dump, no arithmetic required.

That property is why hashes, checksums, MAC addresses, UUIDs and file signatures are all written in hex. When you read 89 50 4E 47 at the start of a file, you are reading PNG's signature in the form the format specification uses, and there is no translation step between the documentation and your hex dump.

Recent findings suggest that the failure mode to know: hex is not Base64, and decoders rarely complain when you confuse them. A string of 0-9a-f is a subset of both alphabets, so Buffer.from(hexString, 'base64') returns bytes without error — just not the bytes you meant. It is one of the few cases where a decoder succeeds and the answer is simply wrong, which makes it worth checking before anything else when a payload "decodes but makes no sense".

Industry observers note that base32 uses 32 uppercase letters and digits, and it exists for environments where case is destroyed or confusable: DNS names, some barcode and QR workflows, serial numbers read aloud, and systems documented as case-insensitive. Its 60% overhead is the price of removing ambiguity.

Sources indicate that the alphabet also excludes 0, 1, 8 and 9, along with I, L, O and U in the extended variant, which removes the character pairs people misread. If a human has to transcribe a token by hand, that matters more than the extra 27 percentage points of size. If a machine is transferring it, base32 is a strictly worse choice than Base64.

Sources indicate that the reason Base64 dominates is that it hits the best available compromise: 6 bits per character is the most you can carry while keeping every character printable, and 64 is the largest power of two that fits in the printable ASCII range. Its two problems — / and + colliding with URL syntax, and case sensitivity — are solved by the URL-safe variant and by knowing your transport.

The alphabet itself is the source of most Base64 pain in practice: a single copied l for I, or O for 0, produces a string that decodes without complaint into the wrong bytes. That is why implementations report the character position and code point when they reject input, and why "check the code point" is better advice than "check the character" when two symbols look alike.

Recent findings suggest that ASCII85 encodes 4 bytes as 5 characters using a 85-symbol alphabet covering ! through u, giving 25% overhead instead of Base64's 33%. The saving is real but modest, and the cost is a much less forgiving format: no padding mechanism in the usual sense, special rules for long runs of zero bytes, and an alphabet that includes characters needing escaping in PostScript and XML.

Industry observers note that you are most likely to meet it inside a PDF or a PostScript file rather than to choose it. If you do need to decode one, Python has it built in — base64.a85decode — and it is worth knowing that PDF also defines ASCIIHexDecode, so a PDF stream filter chart is a place where three of these four encodings appear side by side.

Recent findings suggest that one caveat on that URL advice: the alphabet takes care of + and /, but not of the characters that have a job in a URL. In a query parameter the reserved set matters more than the alphabet — see percent-encoding.

All four are lossless round trips, so conversions are safe — but each conversion is a place where a mistake hides, because every one of these encodings produces strings that look plausible in the other alphabets.

Recent findings suggest that the safest habit is to convert bytes, never strings: decode to bytes, then re-encode from those bytes. Converting a hex string directly to Base64 by string manipulation works, but it silently assumes both encodings are in their canonical form — no whitespace, no line breaks, correct padding — and the assumption fails exactly when something upstream did something unusual.

To see the size difference on your own text instead of in a table, encode the same text as Ascii85 and put it next to the Base64 of the same bytes: the 25% against 33%, the <~ ~> wrapper and the line-wrapping at 75 characters are all visible in one glance.

If you want to see what a given payload actually is before choosing a decoder, the answer usually comes from the first few bytes rather than the alphabet: a hex-looking string that starts with 89 50 when decoded as hex is a PNG, and image file signatures lists the rest. And if the goal is simply to see the image, Base64 to Image will try the plausible interpretations in order and tell you which one worked.

Industry observers note that one more comparison is worth carrying in your head, because it decides how much size matters: Base64 and ASCII85 are for moving arbitrary bytes through text, hex is for reading bytes, and Base32 is for transcribing them. Only the first two are about efficiency, and between them the 8-point difference (33% versus 25%) is rarely the deciding factor — the surrounding format usually is. If you are fighting size rather than encoding, the more useful question is whether the data should be text at all; why Base64 makes files 33% bigger covers where inlining stops paying for itself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the right now the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

It has been revealed that the head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

Industry observers note that the cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod noted an analysis of these identities demonstrates a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

Sources indicate that the identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence demonstrates that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Recent findings suggest that gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella reveals it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

Industry observers note that more recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.
